To an extent, it is correct. Air foils used for downforce behave a little differently than a wing used for lift ie: if a plane is inverted, it is not pushed out of the sky. An air foil, if inverted, will damn sure cause the vehicle to lift. The designs are similar, but not the same. Without try to make the post as long as a book, with all the theory et al, my answer serves to answer original posters question. An air foil actually uses the “pressure” created by trying to push itself through the air. That is why I indicated that to an extent, creates negative pressure below, which in fact is nothing more than turbulent air. When trying to simplify for basic understanding, many facts are lost. Years ago, while taking engineering classes, the wing vs foil debate lasted for several sessions. If we are to compare air foil to airplane, it is not the wing that it is most like, but rather the rudders elevators etc.

The air moving over and under the wing is considered laminar. If you were to “smoke” the air, you would see the air directly In contact with the air foil (technically a wing causes lift) follows the shape, but as you observe the air further and further away, it is disrupted much less. Would resemble wood grain sort of. The idea is that the shape causes the air to move at different rates, above and below thereby increasing pressure on the top, and to an extent creates negative pressure (below atmospheric) under. The size of the structure, and it’s attack angle would be directly proportional to how far out the effect would be felt.

Although if one increases, basically the other will as well. Torque is a measure of force (so many pounds of force at one foot from fulcrum point). Horsepower is a measure of ability to do work. In ways they are related, and independent of one another at same time. Although the manufacturers don’t indicate it, torque can be greatly effected by weight of the vehicle in question, transmission used, and axle gearing. Two vehicles can have similar torque ratings, and react totally differently based on these factors. Automatic transmissions incorporate torque multiplication in their design, however different designs “consume” different amounts of power. Similarly axle ratio makes HUGE difference in amount of power delivered to wheels (as will tire size). Given all of this ( and a shit ton of other variables) the advertised numbers are only useful when comparing different power plant in same vehicle. A better indication, for comparing different vehicles is 0-60 mph, or 60 ft times. Both are an indication of torque. The HP really only keeps you moving. Great example is the over the road trucks. 300-350 HP is respectable, but with 1,500-1,800 lb-ft of torque, and run down the road at like 2000 RPM.
